nova.title: Nova
nova.overview: No-internet schools lack resources for quality education.
nova.approach: Nova: offline learning platform — a device that broadcasts an intranet, giving nearby devices access to an edge computed AI tutor and learning resources including Khan Academy and Ted Talks.
texts: No-internet schools lack resources for quality education.

A handful of underfunded schools in South Sudan and Tanzania, educators complained about unreliable internet, insufficient materials, and difficulty keeping up with changing curriculums. These problems had prevented students from getting into secondary school and pursuing higher education.
A device that broadcasts an intranet (think WIFI), giving nearby devices access to an edge computed AI tutor and learning resources including Khan Academy and Ted Talks.
Shipped to Tanzania and South Sudan
Collecting quantitative data in South Sudan
can connect to Nova at once.

This case study focuses on design for students and teachers with low digital literacy while under high hardware constraints.

A Computer Lab with No Computers, No Internet

There was a room labeled “computer lab”, yet it was collecting dust with no internet and no computers. Aaron couldn’t find the one pic he had, but it looked something like this. Dirt floor, dusty, and it had a chair and an empty desk.
Teachers are often underqualified and schools areunderstaffed.
The government keeps changing curriculums, and teachers have a hard time keeping up.
Schools are underfunded and the government is concerned with internal conflict =
Our non-profit partner LetAllGirls talked with an educator in Tanzania to learn about their current setup.
Teachers lack material to accommodate all students.
"With 50 students in a class, it’s hard to satisfy with the material we have."
Not enough material to go around and limited technology to make up for it.
Difficulty making material for new government curriculum.
"It would be great if we could make new quizzes based on the curriculum."
3+ schools were understaffed and had to create new material manually with outdated tools.
We’ve want lab equipment for students to do hands-on, but we can’t afford that.
Without lab equipment, they can’t do the groupwork described in the new curriculum.
How do we bring quality, up-to-date resources to students + teachers and encourage curious exploration?
The tutor was to be dynamic with not only the curriculum but to each student’s education level.
Help teachers focus on students rather than on constantly reviewing large syllabus updates.
Schools often couldn't afford lab equipment, but teachers wanted to promote group work and hands-on activities.
As opposed to the piles of hyperlinks provided by the RACHEL (only other offline database), our library had to be easy to navigate.
Ask  about what’s on screen. No hopping tabs.
Students hardly benefitted from existing offline databases due resources being dated and difficult to navigate.
(NOVA concept 3D render). Easily update-able, low maintenance, and explorative at a cultural level.
Relied on the fact that students had internet and devices at home, but it's not the case.
Difficult to economically produce at scale.
Existing hardware only supported disorganized hyperlinks to content that wasn't culture-relevant.
Students are curious to do their own research independently.
Students borrow teachers’ phones just to Google search, despite poor connectivity.
Navigating high technical constraints posed by edge computing.
Designers went crazy on whiteboards then discussed with engineers to narrow the scope.
Found core features to focus on according to user needs.
a sharp focus on providing value.
We had to minimize the amount of “beautification” that would cost development time.
A GPU and motherboard in a precarious pose.
We matched each major problem with an approach
Matching the current structure, not disrupting or reinventing.
Teachers were busy updating their material according to new syllabi, so we focused on integration with any teaching style and assignment.
Hardware limited LLM context, so we designed backend for better UX
The budget and hardware lowered our LLM's available tokens. At first, we expected users to press “new conversation” every 5 prompts…
Users would be frustrated at its forgetful nature.

This performance challenge would cost students to halt exploration or getting help on a project. With no room for a full onboarding or an account setup system, each student wouldn’t know the exact function of a simple “new conversation” button.
I sat down with the lead engineer: Could we prevent the LLM from reading everything top-to-bottom to improve latency?

We were able to implement an AI relevance-checking system. Funnily, we had a surplus of storage, so we added an additional "dumb" AI to check and return Y/N, using less computing power and speeding up response generation.
Matching existing habits with similar design patterns

I knew that given 1) their overall lower digital literacy and 2) their very different culture, we’d have to be intentional with each design decision. After interviewing teachers and students, we learned that they were familiar with WhatsApp.
All ages were familiar with WhatsApp
We mimicked WhatsApp’s iconography to improve usability and lean on existing intuition.
Shipped to 2 schools and 1 library for high school students! Unfortunately had to pass off all software to partner without collecting longitudinal data.
Because everyone ends up assuming limitations into existence, hindering creative thinking.
Think with the tech, not around it.
Learning from engineers gives opportunity to design outside of the “technical box”, making limitations less rigid than imagined.
Documenting knowledge on all fronts such as LLM performance and stakeholder goals is key to team alignment and integrated design thinking at every step.
With more funds it could allow learners and teachers to access Adobe Creative Suite, coding platforms, and more.
Make student/teacher accounts so the AI tutor and teachers can understand student progress.
Without the technical constraints, AI that is computed in-house might be the next level of personalization and private security.

nuance.title: Nuance
nuance.overview: The deaf can't hear emotion over the phone without video.
nuance.approach: Nuance: call w/ emotional context — a mobile calling app that pairs animation with live captioning.
texts: The deaf can’t hear emotion over the phone
Conversation is not the words we say—it’s the way we say them. A pause. A laugh. A shift in tone. A raised brow. These small cues carry big emotional weight.
But what happens when those cues are stripped away? That’s what we realized when we spoke to members of the hard-of-hearing community:
A mobile calling app that pairs animation with live captioning.
Introduced an expressive 3D character to give emotional cues
AI analyzes the caller’s tone and other subtle cues to animate the 3D character, communicating emotion.
ASL will be translated to text then voice for the caller on the other end.
This case study focuses on accessibility-first design.
People don't know how to communicate with the hard-of-hearing.
The deaf often resort to messaging even with captions available.
It’s not hard to find a shared problem
Numerous deaf influencers complain about phone calls and captions as a necessity.
Imagine not understanding over 50% of what’s happening around you.
Attitude, tone, and many other conversational nuances are lost.
60% of adults not confident interacting with the deaf.
YouGov survey commissioned by the Royal National Institute for Deaf people.
Current calling apps turn to texting, still losing the emotional clarity.
Captions don’t provide enough context in conversations.
The feeling of a real conversation is lost
“I know what they’re saying, but I can’t feel how they’re saying it.”
The missing nuances in a conversation, from a soft chuckle to a frown, are crucial context clues. Sad? Giddy? Sarcastic?
How do we bring the emotional cues of a real conversation into the calling experience?
Combining visual emotional cues with captioning.
(A mockup of what a standard captioned call feels like).
A live captioning service is paired with an avatar so callers feel understood. Users can use ASL, similar to video calls.
: Can’t make it today Something urgent came up.
oh ok. (unaware she’s sad about it)
: Sorry. I really wanted to see you.
yea... (thinks she might be making excuses)
: Hey, Can’t make it today Something urgent came up.
: No worries! I hope everything’s okay. (Sees sadness). Let me know if you want to talk later
: Sorry. I really wanted to see you. I’ll call you in the evening!
: Sure! Let’s catch up later then. (Sees affection)
Without auditory cues, deaf people rely heavily on facial expressions.
Animation: We can show facial expressions without video.
Despite these being drawn in 2 seconds, you could already interpret each face’s emotion.
AI may evolve to be emotionally intelligent.
AI may not accurately pick up emotions right now, but in the future, AI will be able to detect emotional signals.
I modeled, rigged, and animated an avatar that changed expressions based on the tone, pacing, and other subtle nuances.
The facial expressions aren’t easy to read; we need more clarity.

The more senses that are engaged, the more real the experience becomes. In the same vein, if we layer more sensory information given to the most active sense, sight, they’ll be able to more efficiently analyze context clues.
We can give layer multiple visual emotional cues.
The more cues, the more natural the conversation will feel.
Color is often directly linked to emotion, so we leveraged color as a visual cue for emotion, making facial expressions more easy to interpret.
For example, red has different psychological interpretations across cultures. It can signify love, passion, anger, danger, excitement, and more.
Key Insight: We must give users control over what colors mean.
Color-emotion pairing: Users choose what colors mean to them.
RAG would have to be quite insane for this to work, but I don’t doubt that it will be possible.
Not just plain text transcription, but emotional documentation as well.
We decided that the navbar wasn’t necessary given the speedy product experience. People just want to make a call, not dig through pages.
Mashing different cues build an immersive experience. E.g. design for blind people could layer haptic + auditory cues.
No need to design everything to communicate value.
80% effort in divergent problem-thinking, not throw-away features.
Accessibility is a necessary human right, not another box that has to be ticked off.
Designing with more than one form of sensory feedback.
In my future designs, I will look for ways to increase the number of senses involved in the experience.
